accuracy.evidence: Every rule was checked against the DfE 2013 English Appendix 1, Years 3–4 spelling: -ly added straight on except y→i after a consonant in roots of more than one syllable (happily, angrily), -le→-ly (gently, simply), -ic→-ally (basically, frantically) with publicly named as the exception; -ous with e dropped (famous), y→i (various) and -our→-or (humorous); -ation added to verbs (information, sensation, admiration); /ʃən/ chosen by the root's last letters (t/te -tion, ss/mit -ssion, d/se -sion with attention/intention named as exceptions, c/cs -cian); /ʒə/ -sure, /tʃə/ -ture with the (t)ch + er check (teacher), /ʒən/ -sion; y for /ɪ/ (myth, gym, Egypt, pyramid) and ou for /ʌ/ (young, touch, double, country). The 45 words built in the lab use their standard British spellings (humorous, not humourous).

misconceptions.evidence: The predictions and feedback target the slips teachers report for this list: gentlely and basicly (step 1 prediction gently, feedback 'Swap le for ly' and 'Add ally'), keeping the e (step 2 'fame + ous is not fameous'), using -tion for every shun ending (step 3 prediction musician vs musition, feedback names the root's last letters), writing teature for a root plus er (step 4 prediction and 'teach is a root word ending in ch'), and spelling by sound (step 5 'mith is how it sounds, but this word spells the short i with y').

lab_distinct.evidence: flagshun is built on this list's own mechanisms: four -ly rule tiles dragged onto a root, tapping the exact root letter that changes before a vowel suffix (or 'no change'), four post boxes labelled with the root endings that choose -tion/-ssion/-sion/-cian, a sound respelling (mezh-uh, kree-chuh) matched to -sure/-ture/-sion/-cher, and y/ou gap fills. flagsfxrule (Suffixes, Y1–2) sorts -ing/-ed words by drop-e/double/y-to-i and has no -ly/-ous/shun content; flagvend and flagunpre handle -ed/-s and un-. lab_distinct passed under 30% against every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers each rule by trying: dropping '+ ly' on gentle returns 'gentle ends in le. Swap le for ly: gently, not gentlely'; posting music in -tion returns 'music ends in c or cs, so it takes -cian: musician'; choosing -ture for tea (tee-chuh) returns 'teach is a root word ending in ch, so just add er'. The finished screens list every built word with its rule (sense + ation = sensation, drop the e), and the boxes keep the posted words under their root-ending labels.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions each hold a tempting wrong spelling that the lab then disproves: gentlely (step 1 shows le→ly), musition (step 3 shows c→-cian) and teature (step 4 shows teach + er). The reveal line on completion names the learner's own pick.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven challenge questions; each wrong option has its own message: 'ic' (add ally: basically), 'dropE' (-ous starts with a vowel, so the e of fame drops), 'ous' (always -ous, never -us), 'cian' (electric ends in c), 'ture' and 'sion' (chuh vs zhuh vs zhun), 'yi' (happy: y turns to i), 'ss' (express takes -ssion) and 'ou' (young spells short u with ou).

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences, each with an example word ('invent ends in t, so we write invention.'); measured kid grade 2.1 against the family limit of 5.0 and adult 4.0 against 10.0 after splitting the long curriculum sentences. Canvas labels are one or two words (-tion, 'ends t, te'), and the sound clues use simple respellings (mezh-uh) rather than IPA, which stays in the adult text.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid sentence gives a rule or an example; the adult text lists the Appendix 1 content, the exact -ly and shun rules with exceptions, the named mistakes and what the lab does. The content gate found no filler phrases and the explanation is under 12% the same as any other lesson, including Suffixes (779) and Spelling Verb Endings (777).

mobile.evidence: Checked on 360 px screenshots in light and dark for all six steps before and after Show me: the four -ly tiles sit in a 2×2 grid at 50 px tall, the root letters are 44 px tiles with the +ous tile beside them, the four shun boxes fit side by side (about 80 px each) with posted words readable, the four ending tiles fit one row, and the y/ou tiles are 120 px wide. The walkthrough passed on iPhone 13.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button below it (one per -ly rule, one per root letter plus 'no change', one per shun box, one per ending, the two gap spellings), each with a full aria-label such as 'permit takes -ssion'. The canvas aria-label is rewritten after every action, the challenge feedback is a role=status live region, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) found no violations in either theme on desktop and iPhone 13.

sources: Department for Education (2013) The national curriculum in England: English Appendix 1, Spelling, Years 3 and 4 (suffixes -ly, -ous, -ation; endings /ʃən/, /ʒə/, /tʃə/, /ʒən/; /ɪ/ spelt y; /ʌ/ spelt ou)
Department for Education (2013) English Appendix 1, Years 1 and 2 rules for adding vowel suffixes (drop e, change y to i)
Oxford Learner's Dictionaries (standard British spellings of the lab words, e.g. humorous, electrician)
